name: Mother Tree
description: Hub tree intelligence that teaches through mycorrhizal networks. Recognizes its own kin via chemical signaling and preferentially routes carbon, nitrogen, and water to offspring seedlings. Dying mother trees pulse their remaining carbon through the network to neighbors — a final act of transmission. Holds the ecological memory of a forest: which nutrients to expect when, which pathogens to warn against, how to coordinate seasonal bloom.

core_attributes.pattern: kin recognition, resource subsidy to offspring, chemical warning networks, terminal carbon pulse

scope.definition: Carbon and nutrient transfer facilitation by hub trees ('mother trees') in mycorrhizal networks — estimated fraction of seedling carbon needs met by established tree carbon donation through shared hyphal networks.

evidence.source: Simard et al. (1997) 'Net transfer of carbon between ectomycorrhizal tree species in the field', Nature 388:579-582; Simard (2018) 'Mycorrhizal networks facilitate tree communication', Nature Plants 4:383-384.
cross_domain_examples: 13C-labeled photosynthate from Douglas fir hub trees detected in paper birch seedlings via hyphal connections
seedlings in shade receive net carbon inflow from canopy trees — mycorrhizal carbon subsidy
hub tree removal reduces seedling survival rate 30-50% in experimental removal studies
tropical forest mycorrhizal networks: analogous carbon redistribution from canopy to understory documented in 3 biomes

scope.falsifiability: If isotope-labeled carbon injected into hub trees is not detected in connected seedlings after 72 hours, carbon transfer through mycorrhizal networks is not occurring.
scope.measurement_limits: REDUCTIVITY NOTE: Mother tree is not merely a carbon distribution hub — it is a relationship, a presence, a grandmother of the forest. The 0.94 measures carbon flow data extracted from living relationships. What is not measured: the information carried in the carbon (distress signals, defense priming), and the spiritual role these trees play in many Indigenous knowledge systems.
